---
title: "Multinomial OSA Example"
format: 
  html:
    self-contained: true
---

Simulate some multinomial data with 5 categories.

```{r}
#| echo: true

library(RTMB)

dat <- list()
p_true <- c(0.1,0.5,0.2,0.05,0.15)
np <- 5
size <- 15
dat$X <- rmultinom(100, size = size, prob = p_true)
```

We make inference on the multivariate logit transformed $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$, not $\textbf{p}$. This is unique as we remove a parameter, as given 4 of the 5 proportions, we know the 5 $p_5 = 1-\sum_{i=1}^4 p_i$. One option for transformation is the multivariate logit,

$$
  \boldsymbol{\alpha} = g(\textbf{p}) = \{ \log(p_1/(1-p_5), \dots,  \log(p_4/(1-p_5)\}.
$$
The inverse of this function is then,

$$
  \textbf{p} = g^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \Big\{ \frac{\exp(\alpha_1)}{1+\sum  \exp(\alpha_i)},\ldots, \frac{\exp(\alpha_4)}{1+\sum \exp(\alpha_i)}, \frac{1}{1+\sum \exp(\alpha_i)} \Big\}
$$

Coding this transformation:

```{r}
#| echo: true

mlogit <- function(p){
  np <- length(p)
  log(p[1:(np-1)]/p[np])
}

imlogit <- function(alpha){
  expalpha <- exp(c(alpha, 0))
  expalpha/sum(expalpha)
}
```

Fit the multinomial model and compute the Pearson residuals within the code.

```{r}
#| echo: true

library(RTMB)

## One less parameter as they have to sum to 1
par <- list(alpha = numeric(np-1))

nll <- function (par){
  getAll(par, dat)
  X <- OBS(X)  
  X_raw <- dat$X

  p <- imlogit(alpha)
  ll <- 0
  ## Note can't use ncol(X) as when simulating OSA it isn't a matrix...
  ## Pearson residuals
  res <- matrix(0, ncol = 100, nrow = np)
  
  for(i in 1:100){
    ll <- ll + dmultinom(X[,i], prob=p, log=TRUE)
    res[,i] <- ( X_raw[,i]-size*p )/( sqrt(size*p*(1-p)) )    
  }
  REPORT(res)
  -ll
}

obj <- MakeADFun(nll, par, silent = TRUE)
fit <- nlminb (obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr)

## Report Pearson Residuals
pearson <- obj$report()$res
```

Now let's use RTMB to get the OSA residuals

```{r}
#| echo: true

## One step ahead simulation:
r <- oneStepPredict(obj, method = "oneStepGeneric", observation.name = "X",
  discrete = TRUE, discreteSupport = 0:size, trace = FALSE)
osa <- as.matrix(r$residual, nrow = np, ncol = 100)
```

Now we will compute the randomized quantile residuals assuming independence between each observation. Then do the same thing conditioning on the previous observations, which is equivalent to the OSA residuals.

For the multinomial distribution, a single observation is binomially distributed.

```{r}
#| echo: true

## Randomized Quantile Residuals: Marignal CDF is binomial.
pest <- imlogit(fit$par)
rqr <- NULL
for(j in 1:np){
  pbin <- pbinom(dat$X[j,]-1, size = size, prob = pest[j])
  pbineq <- pbinom(dat$X[j,], size = size, prob = pest[j])
  pq <- runif(ncol(dat$X), pbin, pbineq)
  rqr <- rbind(rqr, qnorm(pq))
}

## Ordered version that is the same as OSA:
## Randomized Quantile Residuals: Conditional CDF is binomial.
osa_manual <- NULL
psum <- 1
Xsum <- numeric(nrow(dat$X))
for(j in 1:(np-1)){
  pless <- pbinom(dat$X[j,]-1, size = size - Xsum, prob = pest[j]/psum)
  peq <- pbinom(dat$X[j,], size = size - Xsum, prob = pest[j]/psum)
  pq <- runif(ncol(dat$X), pless, peq)
  osa_manual <- rbind(osa_manual, qnorm(pq))
  Xsum <- Xsum + dat$X[j,]
  psum <- psum - pest[j]
}

```

Plot them all to compare

```{r}
#| echo: true

par(mfrow = c(1,4))
qqnorm(pearson, main = "Pearson Residuals (QQ)")
qqline(pearson)

qqnorm(rqr, main = "RQR Residuals (QQ)")
qqline(rqr)

qqnorm(osa[-np,], main = "OSA Residuals (QQ)")
qqline(osa[-np,])

qqnorm(osa_manual, main = "Manual OSA Residuals (QQ)")
qqline(osa_manual)

```
